Without protective measures, the cases over time will go up quickly and go down a little more over time. John D. O'Bryant School of Math and Science.

When examining this graph, I think an appropriate headline for this graph will be "Learning to flatten out the curve for COVID-19 cases"

I am a student from the John D. O’Bryant School of Math and Science School!

raw_comment:
At first glance, without protective measures seemed to be the better option to me. The faster we can all get over this virus, the better things will be. But thinking more about it I realized how selfish that was. You can see that taking these protective measures may make the virus last longer, but people are safer and will have better access to treatment. I've been ignorant enough to believe that neither me nor any of my loved ones will be effected by this virus. If someone I cared about got the virus and died, I would be extremely upset, but at least I would know we did all we could to protect them. The time frame of the virus passing has no importance to the lives being lost.

After reading "The Reveal" and "Stat Nuggets" for the graph, I realized it wasn't literal, but instead a way to show people how important it is to take these protective measures. The information shown was no real data because it didn't take into account any death rates, or age, or previous medical trouble, it was theoretically based on previous epidemics. You cant predict or prevent these events from happening, but you can take precautions and raise awareness for the level of threat that these pandemics cause.

raw_comment:
After reading the reveal, I learned that I was focusing on the wrong part of the graph. Instead of worrying about keeping the curve flat, I was creating hypothetical situations about what would happen if the healthcare system was exceeded. I also assumed that the graph was based off some data collected in the United States, while in reality it was all theoretical and only emphasizing the importance of "flattening the curve." I understand that mitigation is so important in reducing the number of cases, but I have concern for the state of the economy after the virus is contained. By flattening the curve, we will see less cases and less deaths, but will the global economic repercussions be worth those lives. Now, I'm not saying the economy is more important than people's lives, but a moral dilemma arises: save a thousand lives from the virus, or potentially lose millions from the aftermath. 

The reveal brought a perspective to my eyes about this graph. Instead of focusing on the y-axis, or the number of cases, I looked at the x-axis, or the time till the virus is gone. With proper mitigation and safety precautions taken, the curve can potentially stay below the healthcare capacity. This would be vital in our attempt to subdue the virus, even though the virus may exist longer. Ultimately, how we handle this virus, and the actions we take as a country, and as a globe, will be a defining part in history.

raw_comment:
Looking at my original thoughts and the "Reveal", I do see a few things contradictory to what I said. My original opinion was that the second curve was based on pure mathematics and calculations, but after reading the reveal, I now see that it is way more theoretical than that. First, the idea that the second curve will not exceed the healthcare system's ability is not certain. The graph is theoretical, based on other pandemics and rational thought, but not a certain curve that our country will get if we use the protective measures. However, I agree and understand the curve and know that it is achievable with the introduction of the protective measures.

Another thing is that I knowingly went off topic in my previous comment. I talked more about the time being used and how that would also affect the country. While I still believe this is important, I think that I should have focused more on the amount of infections, our health care systems ability, and how the introduction of the protective measures will help our country. Our country, like many others, has many cases, but we weren't the first ones. We should be looking at other countries to see what they are doing that works. China is a prime example and has used protective measures and lock downs to slow the curve. We now know it can be slowed and should do all we can to follow as they did to ensure the most American's safety.

raw_comment: Before the reveal, I assumed that the graph was based off of a certain set of data, not necessarily just an info-graphic to persuade users to take precautionary measures. Although the graph is not based off of data, it still provides a great visual to remind us our part in preventing the spread of the coronavirus. Another part of the graph that I payed more attention after the reveal was how the "with protective measures" graph reached the x axis much later than the "without protective measures" graph. I had to think about it, but it absolutely made since after I did. Taking precautionary measures to slow down the spread of the virus will increase the period of when a large number of people have it, it will just decrease how many people have it at a time. This is important so hospitals and other facilities maintain enough resources to treat those affected.

raw_comment:
Looking at this graph, it is pretty self explanatory what is happening. With the introduction of protective measures the number of cases will not exceed what the healthcare system can handle, and while the process will be more slow, overall it is the best and safest way to protect our society during this crisis.
Looking at this, I notice that this is just an idea of what could happen and it isn't set in stone which curve our country is going to take. However, based on all of the steps our country has made to limit social interaction, I think that we are bound to take the second curve. As long as the country stays  abides by what law enforcement has said, our curve will not exceed healthcare's line, and we will suffer many less deaths because of that. 
I also have to wonder, is there anything else that our country can be doing to ensure we have that curve? We have shut down almost everything in the country, put many places into lock down, and stopped almost all social interactions in areas that have the most risk. Overall, I think our country has done almost flawlessly, but it also leads me to think what consequences might come from choosing this curve instead of the other one? There will be less death, but the economy will be suffering longer with everyone in lockdown. This could put us into a big recession and ruin our economy. It begs the question, is the suffering of the virus's effects worse than the effects we will receive from trying to stop this country altogether?

raw_comment:
After only  seeing the graph I actually started asking my mom questions about the Covid-19 virus since she is an ED nurse. She explained a lot of the same things the article did. She told me how the hospital's around the world are doing everything they can to get Covid-19 patients in and out of the hospital to decrease the curve of the graph. She also told me about all of the safety procedures everyone around the world should be going through. All this graph did was put it in perfect perspective for me.
The article talks about how without flattening this curve hospitals around the  world would be overflowing with patients and how almost double the amount of people would be infected without proper sanitation.

raw_comment:
When I first looked at the graph I was very surprised on how the number of cases went down when protective measures were taken. As I read the article I realized how powerful it is. The article described that when you take action quickly you can reduce the spread. I now see the graph as how far we have come doing our part during this virus.

I have also been realizing that even though we are taking the right measures to stop the virus, the right measures are causing people to be out of work and have no income coming in. The virus is not only taking peoples lives but also lessening the economy. I think that that graph should have also incorporated the economy and how many people are out of work.

raw_comment:
It never posted on the 27th so I'm posting it again: 
When I looked at the graph for the first time I thought I understood it completely. After I read the revel and stat nuggets article, looking back at the graph I understand it better. The revel states that the graph shows what could happen if people take protective measures such as social distancing and self-quarantine during the spread of this pandemic, Covid-19. And “does not show how many infected people there are, how many will recover, or how many will die” it is purely to show people why taking proactive measures does matter. I didn't know this when I first looked at the graph. I thought maybe it was a graph from another pandemic such as the spanish flu. The moderator's comments about the graph made me better understand exactly what it shows. I already knew that with proactive measures we can decrease the amount of cases but I didn't know that even with just “moderate interventions, the death rate can be cut in half”. While I was reading the article “Stat Nuggets” I came to understand that the mathematical model “Flattening the Curve Graph” does not predict whether interventions will 100% ensure that people who need medical care won't exceed the health care systems capacity. But the number of cases due to the pandemic won't exceed the number of cases the healthcare system can handle.

raw_comment:
Unlike many others, when I first saw the graph, the first thing that came to my mind  was "propaganda".  It reminds me of the graphs the USSR put out after Chernobyl, no real data, no real meaning, simply two scenarios designed to scare people into falling into line.  It really says nothing mathematical but comes off to most as mathematical which is scary to think.  
This graph is a theory, not based on any evidence of any kind yet is presented in a way that most see to be fact.  Whilst the theory may be correct, that diminishing the number of cases at the start would assist our health care system in treating those who are critically ill, it also has a negative side effect to it.  The longer this virus is around, spreading, the longer the world is stopped.  The longer people are imprisoned at home.  The longer students are out of school.  The longer factories are stopped.  The longer the virus has to mutate.  The longer people are living off the government.  The longer we lose our rights. 

While flattening the curve may mitigate the number of deaths, it may kill the economy even more.  It's a toss up, save a few hundred million globally from dying, or save a few billion from losing everything.  Save a few thousand while 30 million lose the right to work, 70 million lose the  right to leave their home, and the country falls into a depression that may take five to ten years to recover from.  Humanity or sustainability?  Few thousand dead or a few thousand businesses closed.

raw_comment:
First of all, after reading the reveal, I am very surprised that the graph was published as one to use as a basis because I know many people who have based their opinions about the virus off of that graph. I also wonder what “protective measures” really entails. Is it what they described in the Reveal or is it more drastic than that? I am quite proud that someone from Portsmouth, NH was listed in the “Catchy Headlines.”
	In response to some of the questions posed, first, I think that the length of the epidemic will increase with protective measures because instead of everyone getting infected at once, people will be slowly exposed. Some interventions that would decrease the number of fatalities is by spreading the cases out over time, which would mean people must practice protective measures. In all, after the reveal, I am reminded of how people can take such little bits of information and create such deep impressions and ideas with that information. Because of that, I think that the media should be aware of this and try to put out information that is as representative of the situation as possible.

raw_comment: This graph has been all over social media, the news, and other platforms so I was aware of the general meaning behind the graph. However, the extra discussion helped me learn more nuances about the graph that I discovered when I dug into the Star Nugget articles.  The one that interested me the most was The Exponential Power of Now.  On the surface, the graph makes you think about repercussions for different approaches by entire communities - either taking action or not. The article was impactful, because it points out the power of taking action quickly.  Delaying social distancing increases cases by 40%.  Said differently acting now, reduces cases by 40%.  This turns the negative of exponential growth into a positive because people can take action to stop it.

raw_comment: After reading the reveal, I was surprised to find that it did not include any number of cases or death rates. The reveal was more about the impact that preventative measures can have on the disease replication rate and how spreading can be prevented. The reveal was a very good, concise rundown of what can be done to limit the negative effects of covid-19.

raw_comment:
Before the reveal, I looked at the graph as a commendation. I thought the graph was a representation of how COVID-19 was already affecting the United States. However, after the reveal, I now realize that it is a theoretical mathematical model, created by specialists like Dr. Harris from the article. Looking back at the comments of others and the moderator, though, many people seemed to hold my prior thought: that the US was doing a very good job controlling the coronavirus. People thought we were already following the blue curve, when in fact it should be what we aspire to, not what we congratulate ourselves on achieving.
         Looking at the article, "flattening the curve" becomes seemingly even more important. If the peak number of cases can be kept under the healthcare system's capacity, the outbreak is much more manageable. Looking at graphs of each country's cases, however, it is evident that the US will need to do more in order to get on track to follow the blue curve. The early numbers of cases in the US are such that numbers may rise high enough to meet the red curve, which could be catastrophic. A better job must be done distributing testing kits, quarantining those infected, and continuing social distancing. Some seem to think the outbreak is slowing, that it is okay to slacken social distancing. This is untrue. It is important as ever to continue social distancing to slow the spread of the virus, follow the blue curve, and avoid chaos.

raw_comment: The reveal described, in no uncertain terms, the level of influence we all have in terms of spreading the virus. We owe it to ourselves and to our communities to practice social distancing and self-isolation. The reveal provides statistical backing to this claim. Multiple simulations have shown that even small day to day changes can have a measurable effect on the spread of the virus. What was most striking to me about the reveal was the extent to which statistical analysis proves the effectiveness of intervention methods. By comparing the spread of the virus in different countries, with the explanatory variable being government mandated interventions, it is clear that countries with aggressive systems in place in order to fight the disease experience a far slower spread of the virus. After thinking about this model I find myself wondering what the distribution of coronavirus cases in America will look like at the end of the pandemic.

raw_comment:
Before the reveal, I knew that there was a large difference in death rates with or without protective measures, but I did not know that even with moderate precautions, death rate can be cut in half. Of course, these simulations/models are very sensitive to all kinds of variables. I wonder how we can stop or block these. variables... I still wonder how the decrease in the infection spread rate makes the epidemic last longer. If there were no protective measures followed, the epidemic would pass over in a quicker time span. Obviously, we know we still do not want that because it would exceed the healthcare system limit. But how does following protective measures almost double the timeline of the virus? The graph still makes it clear why it is important to follow protective measures ASAP like cancelling public gatherings and school. 
Also - I am very proud of my classmate Evan from Portsmouth, NH for being mentioned in a NYTimes reflection. Your headline was creative and deserved that honorable mention. Very good Evan!

raw_comment: After reading the reveal for this graph and the “Stat Nuggets”, I definitely understand the concept of a mathematical model much better. Before, I knew that the graph was not based on any data from the coronavirus, but I still misunderstood certain specifics behind the graph’s meaning. For one, I thought that the peak of the “with protective measures” curve meant that the model predicted that with interventions our health care system will not be overwhelmed by the number of patients in need of attention. With a stat nugget, I discovered that while the model does predict this circumstance to be less likely, it by no means ensures this outcome. Mathematical models such as this one are very helpful in making decisions on the steps to take in “flattening the curve” and other similar situations, but it’s crucial to understand that they are purely prediction based. There is no definite or one hundred percent certain prediction that can be made; these models simply show the most likely outcomes based on previous patterns and knowledge.

raw_comment: The piece of information that interested me the most after seeing the reveal was that the model was purely theoretical. That model is based on no data at all, it is just to help explain easily what could happen in self-isolation. I thought that the Flatten the Curve graph took into account actual data, but now I realize that this would be almost impossible to model realistically.  It also interested me that this model was based on past worldwide epidemics. This begged the question, "what epidemics are the model based on," and "is that data really reliable." The only pandemics that were as worldwide as COVID-19 is today were the Spanish Flu and Sars. I wonder if it is valid to compare other epidemics that happened at various times in history to an epidemic happening in 2020.

We keep hearing #FlattenTheCurve #FlattenTheCurve, but that line puts it explicitly: staying home will literally save lives. raw_comment:
Now that I have seen the Stat Nuggets, everything has changed for me. Originally, I saw the graph as one not of prediction, but one of exact answers, and the Stat Nuggets immediately disprove that. The graph is just a prediction with no guaranteed answers and no concrete difference between the number of infected people based on interventions. Flattening the curve is obviously something that needs to happen to protect the world, but the data from the graph is not from an actual situation and instead from a prediction. 

Flattening the curve, whether it keeps us under the healthcare threshold or not, is still important because it gives the most people the highest chance of survival. Sure, the virus will occur for longer because it won't burn through patients as fast, but it will ensure that our healthcare systems are not completely overwhelmed with the number of patients. If we let everyone get infected, we would have to fight the disease without any hospital help and simply rely on our immune systems, which is very dangerous. 

Based on the simulation, it is definitely still necessary to practice social distancing and even possibly lead into forced quarantine. People think that "people under the age of 40 and above the age of 5" will be ok because of their developed immune systems, but my mother, who works in the medical field, says that the affects on all age groups is irreparable.

raw_comment:
I have always been big on statistics and facts, which is why I was excited for the statistical reveal of this graph. I thought that there would be more numbers, statistical tests, and, for lack of better words, more "factual" information in the reveal. This graph, however, wasn't based on scientific studies or mathematical projections, but rather observations and theoretical sense. That doesn't make the graph, or the message that it is showing, any less important.

I've been hearing about flattening the curve since Coronavirus was a thing people were making memes about on Instagram. My parents have explained the concept to me and made sure that I understood why it was so important for our community, country, and even the whole world. As it says in the article, "flattening the curve keeps society going". 

Something that caught my eye in the article was the transmission paragraph when discussing how to turn the red curve into the blue curve. The article stated that even though the transmission could be compared to that of seasonal flu, many people are already immune to seasonal flu through antibodies (your body's naturally acquired form of immunity) or vaccines. raw_comment: After reading more into the articles, the reveal, and the moderators' comments,  I can now understand the article more. I see that the graph was based off of just a general idea of the cases and not spot on data. When looking at the results, I understand how to keep the numbers down and help flattening out the curve. They would want to prevent a surge in cases that way the healthcare systems won’t be overwhelmed. And if the number of cases are lower than there give the healthcare officials and workers more of an opportunity to find solutions and cure because their hands aren’t as full as they would be if protective measures weren’t taken by people. Though I do wonder if situations like these have been on the public health community’s mind for years now, why are we not as prepared and why is it not being taken as seriously by some people as it is by others. And though we want to keep the numbers down that may not be an option because as the U.S we are one country out of many, and all may not be playing their part in practicing protective measures.

raw_comment:
When writing my first comment about this graph, I pretty much knew what was going on in it, having seen it when my parents had sent it to me before. What I didn’t know was just how many factors also went into real life data. In my opinion, I was thinking that the graph would be super accurate to what would happen if all people started to take preventative measures, and it would basically be the same, but there are many more things in the real world to factor in, not making it as perfect. 
After reading the Reveal and Stat nuggets, I was left realizing that while even if we do take preventative measures, the number of cases still could be above that line, more than the healthcare system can handle. I also know that cases and death rates would also still be decreased by a great amount, which should be reason enough for everyone to be more aware of everyday things. For example, washing their hands or using hand sanitizer after touching gross surfaces and not touching their face after, like the man in the article. 
To sum up, I don’t see the graph too differently from how I saw it in my first comment, but I now realize how many factors go into this pandemic, with who is more likely to get it or to die, and I see that the real-life graph wouldn’t be as perfect.

raw_comment:
When I first looked at this graph, I felt it was already apparent what I was reading. It says it right there in the red and blue. This is the curve with protective measures. This is the curve without. Then we look towards the axes and we see "# of Cases" over "Time".
 In other words, it's a mathematical model- a prediction, an assumption- of what might happen in 2 different pandemic scenarios. One where we're lenient. One where we're active.
 It was neat reading about the origins of this model, and I enjoyed getting to know a bit more about what it meant and who it came from, but it all feels so unnecessary to me. This graph is extremely thorough, quite frankly, and I really felt that no explanation was needed.
 The graph just screams: "stay at home so our healthcare system doesn't overflow with patients!"

raw_comment:
Unlike I had predicted, the graph is not based on data but shows what the numbers would most likely be if proactive measures were taken. In this ‘reveal’ article, it tells us that the graph was made to show us why we need to take these proactive measures and stay safe. This article states that “The mathematical model behind this dynamic graph predicts that even with moderate interventions, the death rate can be cut in half,” which gives me hope. They also discuss the fact that there is a graph showing the number of new cases in countries with over fifty confirmed cases. Basically, we got this, but we really do need to take these proactive measures and practice social distancing. 
In the Stat Nuggets for “Why We Need To Keep The Curve Flat,” they tell us that “The Flattening the Curve graph is a theoretical mathematical model based on what scientists and staticians have observed from prior epidemics. The model predicts that, if there are proactive interventions, the number of cases in any time period will be less likely to exceed the health care capacity system.” This tells us that again, like I said, we need to take these proactive measures and take care of ourselves and others! This virus will be so much more contained and less intense if we just followed these precautions. Honestly, reading the article and viewing the moderators comments made me see the graph differently because I didn’t realise that the graph wasn’t based on data.

raw_comment: One of the first things that stood out to me when I read the reveal is that this graph was not created based on statistics; rather, it was created as an approximation of what preventative measures against the Coronavirus can do for us. I initially thought that this was a graph that mathematical model that had the x and y axes removed for the sake of allowing us to guess what the real numbers were. However, I now understand that this is more of a theoretical model based on past experiences than it is a statistical model. Another part of this article that caught my eye is how much variation there is to this model depending on many different factors, such as age distribution, fatality rate, and replication rate. Even with how much of our attention is dedicated to this virus right now, we have very little idea of what the overall death total will look like or a solid prediction of what this virus may do.

raw_comment:
Part 1

My first thoughts of the mathematical model presented to us, were how vague it was, and how it lacked some of the necessary information to show an accurate representation of the Curve. Information such as how the “x” and “y” axis are presented based on the age distribution in the U.S. Or the effects put in place to stop the spread of the virus, like travel bans, and mandatory quarantines of returning visitors. But learning that he Model was more hypothetical than an actual prediction of the spread of the virus, and death rate. The comments from the moderators have opened up my eyes to the fact that this model was based on prior epidemics, and is still in question whether as to how much interventions could cut down the death rate of the virus. raw_comment:
After reading through the Reveal as well as the Stat Nugget I feel like what I understood from the original graph was a bit more convoluted than I expected. It was easy enough to understand that we need to take precautions to not spread the virus and that is what will keep the number of cases down but then I realized that the graph was based on hypothetical data. 

Factoring in real precautions is going to be much different than factoring hypothetical precautions. The data of the graph does make logical sense but in what way will we know how extreme precautions need to be to keep the number of cases below their limit like the graph displays. We are taking many precautions now by limiting large scale social interactions but will that be enough to keep the number of cases at bay?

raw_comment:
Reading the moderator’s comments helped me understand the graph a little bit more. Looking at the mathematical model before reading the moderator’s comments, I had a pretty good idea of what the graph was representing. My questions weren’t really answered, but it explained to me that it was a prediction rather than actual data. I understand that flattening the curve is essential with viruses like the Coronavirus, even if it takes longer to get rid of. The epi curves are trying to depict that we need to try and slow down the spread of the virus and keep the # of cases under the Healthcare system capacity.  
    I thought it was interesting that the curve was created by a man who got the virus at an airport bar. He decided to create it to spread awareness and was pleased to see that he sparked some interest in flattening the curve. I think that it is smart to flatten the curve even if it means that the virus is here for longer. It ensures less deaths and give us more control over a situation that seems uncontrollable.

raw_comment:
When writing my original comment, I could get the general idea of this article correct: Less deaths will occur and the virus will be more easily manageable with protective measures. Now, after reading The Reveal and Stat Nuggets, I see that the graph was theoretical and there are many more things that factor into this risk. The article mentions that the graph is not literal, but the consequences could be a lot more severe depending on who followed these protective measures. 
 
The article states that “even with moderate interventions, the death rate can be cut in half.” Of course the problem of Covid-19 is unpredictable and ever growing, but the graph is meant to demonstrate “flattening the curve” and the maintainability of the virus if people practice protective measures. Although, we must not only do our part for our own sake, but to help all the responders who are risking their lives to help those suffering from the virus. By limiting their workload and being responsible during this time, we can help limit the number of cases in such a short period of time that put a strain on our health care system. 

This graph may not be literal, but it is very real. We as citizens can help ourselves and our country to overcome this pandemic. This is why it is so important, as the article mentions, to limit large gatherings, cancel events, stay home, and wash your hands. By doing this, we will be able to save many lives.

raw_comment:
By implementing protective measures, I think the number of cases at any one time would decrease because it slows the rate of infection. This also explains why the epidemic lasts longer because everyone will be infected at a slower rate. 

Interventions that could be instituted to change the outcomes shown in the graph:

time since first case: reducing protective measures so that people are infected at a faster rate or vice versa.

number of cases: fail to quaratine those who are already infected and allow them to roam freely in order to increase cases, put in place even stricter policies to reduce.

health care capability: invest more money into the health care system to help the number of patients treated, divest money to do the opposite.

I think the easiest of these changes to implement would be to allow people to continue to roam around and do whatever they want causing infections to increase while the lenght of the epidemic decreases. The hardest to implement would be to put in place even stricter protective measures to reduce the infection rate as well as increase the time since first case.

raw_comment: All of the curves with the exception of the attempted quarantine curve were as symmetrical as the New York Times graph. The reason I think the quarantine graph is not symmetrical is because the quarantine essentially creates two separate graphs, one of initial infection, then a second outbreak after quarantine. Naturally, the first outbreak is small and is easily brought down. However, when the second outbreak occurs, it hits harder, producing a curve much larger than the previous one, hence why as a whole it is asymmetrical in nature. The amount of intervention I support would be high levels of social distancing, which calls for only 1 in 8 people traveling and greatly reducing the infection rate while greatly increasing the recovery rate.

raw_comment:
What I noticed from this article was how drastically the graph differentiates between taking precautions and not taking precautions. Of course, it is a known fact that often times when there is a precaution taken to ensure something, the result is what we desired, in this case, to stop the cases of Coronavirus. I saw how drastically the curve changed from it going from a high curve to a flattened out curve. And through this graph one can obviously guess that when people are keeping a social distance or maintaing the quarantine rule then there will be less number of cases.

I wonder however that if we were to completely restrict everything strictly, would that result in an extreme and sudden drop in cases or is this something that has to happen gradually regardless of how sudden and strict precaution you take.

 "The only time a Flatline is what we need." or "Keep it safe to Keep it Low." Basically the graphs are showing how people need to follow the mandate of keeping social distance and to take all safety precautions to make sure our curve is more flattened.

I think the original article and the moderator's comments really help open up people's eyes as to how bad and crazy this could get quickly. We see the line that indicates the capacity that the healthcare services can provide services until they themselves can't help people anymore. It is beware type warning for people to follow the rules so we don't have to face that situation, which we unfortunately already are.

raw_comment:
This graph at first glance, without any context, is hard to understand. It’s clear how easy it is to misinterpret just by looking at how many different opinions there were on the graph. Even though I knew it was theoretical, there were too many missing factors in the graph for me to understand exactly what the theory was intending to say. Amongst those factors the writer’s state death rate, recoveries or number of infections. The last of those factors confused me because I thought that was being represented by the vertical axis of the graph, so now I’m not sure what it’s meant to be.
Knowing the graph depicts the rate at which the number of CoronaVirus cases increases over time, this graph is much easier to apply and understand through our current situation. As stated, the graph is used to create a statistical understanding to guide decisions. The theory this graph represents is the one forcing strict quarantine and protective measures, as countries come to the conclusion that these protective measures will slow down the spread. The one thing I still have yet to understand is why it is predicted that the virus will last longer with protective interventions. There are not many factors addressed by the graph so I can’t understand how that prediction came to be.

raw_comment:
After reading The Reveal, Stat Nuggets, and the original article, I think my original assumptions based on the theoretical mathematical model were partially wrong. I understood what the graph was saying, but I didn’t draw the right conclusion from it. The article explained that there would be a higher death rate and widespread panic if we didn’t take preventative measures, which I had sort of understood, but only when I read it did I realise just how bad that could be. People are already hoarding toilet paper, and I would hate to imagine what it would be like if people thought it was a given that they would get the virus.

When I first saw it, the graph seemed very incomplete, and after looking at Stat Nuggets, I can see why. It’s meant to be theoretical, so it says nothing about duration or the extent to which the virus will affect the population. It could be completely wrong, as well. No matter what preventative measures we take, we can’t say how well the healthcare system will be able to address the issue. Healthcare professionals could also get sick, or they might not have the right tools to prevent deaths or spreading of the virus. It’s not mentioned in the article, but the graph also doesn’t take into account the possibility of a second wave of the virus after the quarantine ends. All of this makes the graph just a little sketchy.

raw_comment:
I probably haven’t been concerned enough about the virus. Beforehand, I understood that healthy people were transmitting the disease and that our healthcare systems were preparing to be overrun, but looking at the models from the Washington Post really helped me grasp the transfer of COVID-19. 
My original comment stands true to the information after the reveal- if we take protective measures, we can slow the spread of the disease. We must flatten the curve. But when I was writing the comment I didn’t understand how important this was. Looking at the Washington Post models, if we social distance, we will be able to control the virus and flatten the curve. We will be in it for the long haul because the spread of the disease will go much slower (and it will continue to spread), but we might just be able to scrape by without overrunning the healthcare system.
Of course, these models provide no guarantee that won’t happen anyway. But if we can prevent doctors from becoming ill themselves, if we can prevent doctors from having to choose which has to die, we must be willing to be uncomfortable in our social distancing, we must be willing to stop going places. Because even if you yourself aren’t sick, someone else you see might be, and then you might carry the disease to someone at risk. That’s why it’s important to eliminate the temptation to be out and socializing in public areas, why we should close public places, as the article says. We will have a chance to save more people.

raw_comment:
Initially, I thought the graph was supporting the idea that we will get over this epidemic faster if we do not implement protective measures. After reading “The Reveal,” and analyzing the graph some more it was more clear that this graph was predicting the number of cases of corona correlated to the protective measures and how these protective measures work to flatten the curve, or decrease the number of cases. The Stat Nugget helped me understand that the information is correlative not literal, since these are mathematical estimations based on previous epidemic data.

It’s important that our health officials and staff do not feel overwhelmed during this time and that they have enough medical equipment to treat everybody; therefore, it is clear that protecting as many people as possible no matter the length of time, is the right decision that our country is making.

In order for us to flatten the curve effectively, we, as citizens, are the first line of defense and we need to start defending better. We hold the power to combat and stop this disease from spreading, so we need to use that power. I like the line that was highlighted in the article by Lilly, stating, “protect our healthcare system by protecting yourself.” Like the article mentions, canceling school and public gatherings, and preparing hospitals have helped us control the spread of this disease, and we should continue the practices suggested by health care officials.

raw_comment:
At first glance of this graph a few days ago, I noticed that everything researchers, scientists, doctors, and public officials were saying was true to a significant extent. Remaining at home and social distancing yourselves from as many people as possible will indefinitely lower the curve. With an open mindset but a more serious one as well, I now notice more about the healthcare system capacity not just across America, but across the world. The curve titled "Without Protective Measures" completely breaks the line for our healthcare system. When I look at this line, I see one that's not strong and bold, but rather already dotted. This makes me wonder if the graph is trying to make a point by showing people that the healthcare system can be broken. In fact, it will be broken if we don't take serious measures, everyone included, to stop the spread of this pandemic. 

A lot is going on in this graph. Some people may just see two simple opposing curves where one breaks through a line and one does not. But others, who really care and look closely, may see that the "With Protective Measures" curve almost touches the health care system capacity line. This tells us something of very high importance- doing everything we can to stay healthy, stay educated, and taking the most precautious measures may not even be enough in itself. But it's surely our only chance at preventing the number of cases from continuously growing exponentially. 

I would title this graph "A Break in the Curve."

raw_comment:
The revealed article was able to make me look differently at and better understand the information that the model wanted to provide to us. Prior to reading this article, I tried to attach forms of real data to the model, when that wasn’t the intent. This article shows the importance of managing the surge of infection, with the model showing us the difference between good and bad trends of illness and infection. 

The model shows what would be an unprotected society’s curve in red. These high surges are what we want to avoid most. The blue curve shows what our aim is, in order to keep more people healthy and make things much more manageable. Being able to mitigate the spread of illnesses is very important, because it gives us more time to stop the disease completely and put less lives at risk. The coronavirus’ openness to spreading is most troublesome compared to other similar sicknesses like the flu. This is why mitigation is so important, by decreasing the number of people the virus can spread to through social distancing we have already begun to work towards stopping the virus. We need to stay aware of our surroundings in order to stay as healthy as possible, but we are already beginning to flatten the curve in order to keep our communities safe.

I was right this article said that the old graph wasn’t based on any real data; it was just an estimate of what could happen if we didn’t take protective measures. Do news outlets and the government do this often, has this happened in the past, does this method of keeping people safe work?

raw_comment: Although before reading the reveal I was aware of the importance of quarantining, I am even more aware than I was before. Although it seems like it is not a big deal to go out and hang out with a few friends right now, or even run a quick errand, social distancing will show benefits in the future. If one person thinks it is okay for them to go out, then chances are many more people are thinking that same thought. This causes more people to go out, which just increases the risk of more people getting infected. Right now, the cancelling of schools, flights, and public gatherings is helping to keep the curve flat and allow for hospitals to be better prepared so that as a country we don't exceed our healthcare system's capacity. Although it may seem pointless now, staying home and keeping your distance from others is not just saving the lives of people who may die, but is also helping everyone who is affected by this quickly spreading virus.

raw_comment:
(Part 2)
In my own state, the cases increase every day along the logistic model (as of this morning, we have 763 confirmed cases, but surely we all understand that not everyone is tested and for a case to be “confirmed” it has to be checked with the CDC in addition to the doctor/nurse who administered the test). We’ve so far had 3 people die, one a day for the last three days. I can’t help but wonder how this could be much worse if we hadn’t taken any action and how this can be kept to the bare minimum if we stick to our social-distancing. Maybe this means the events we miss will continue to be cancelled and we’ll be working from home for a while, but if it saves lives and helps our hospitals, I think it’s definitely a price worth paying.

raw_comment:
When I initially looked at this graph last week, I understood it as the importance of following protective measures at the time of a pandemic.  I believed it showed how practicing social distancing and good hygiene can save the lives of others.  The graph encouraged me to stay away from large crowds and to wash my hands constantly.  Due to Covid-19 being in the United States for such a short period of time, I predicted that the graph was only based on mathematical predictions.  There has not been enough data gathered to prove the validity of the graph and that is why there are no numbers and statistical increments on the graph.  

The “Reveal”, published on the 26th of March, backed up my previous claims.  The graph is simply a mathematical model based on data from previous epidemics.  It should be used to gain qualitative and/or quantitative understanding and not be taken entirely literally by the public.  Scientists use these hypothetical graphs to keep the public informed and to encourage them to practice the suggested protective measures.  It represents the impact Covid-19 will have in America if we don’t follow protective measures versus if we do.  The graph shows how valuable interventions are when fighting a virus.  Interventions like drive-through testing, cancellation of public gatherings, school closings, and preparation of hospitals greatly slow the spread of Covid-19.  These precautions will decrease the infection rate and deaths across the nation.

raw_comment:
(Part 1)
We need protective measures to limit the cost of this virus. This was made even more clear to me after reading over The Reveal and Stat Nuggets. It can be really frustrating being separated from the people you love for so long, stuck in your house, but it’s worth it. The article predicts that even with moderate interventions, the death rate can be cut in half; imagine how many lives can be saved if we take more extreme measures! If we restrict interaction to the very minimum, we’re less likely to come into contact with infected people and/or items; the illness will be contained, or the spread will at least not be quite so rampant. And no matter how much interaction we have, it is vital that we be very meticulous with our hygiene. Hand-washing, while simple, goes a long way. A simple bleach solution to spray on door handles and gas pumps is also a great example of potentially life-saving cleanliness.

raw_comment: The Flattening the Curve Graph is based on prior epidemics which makes it a theoretical mathematical model of the Coronavirus. The goal, of course, is to flatten the curve with the least possible deaths while, also, staying under the healthcare capacity line. The article provides a fairly simple solution to making sure that we reach our goal, and that is, social distancing. New York, or more specifically, New York City, is a fair representation of the red curve, and in order to mitigate it into the more reasonable blue curve, we need to take some precautionary measures. With social distancing, there will be less people packed in one place which will ultimately slow down the spread of the disease. There will not be so much as a surge of cases that overload hospitals, so we will be able to control and handle the virus much better which means less deaths. To explain the idea more clearly, the article compares it to a subway car during rush hour. The subway car is the hospital, and it can only take so many “patients” at a time, so the rest have to wait at the platform. By staggering work hours (practicing social distancing), the rush hour will be less of a rush since less people are in need of the subway car at one time, so people are more likely to be able to get on the car and have a comfortable ride.

raw_comment: When I looked at the graph for the first time I thought I understood it completely. After I read the revel and stat nuggets article, looking back at the graph I understand it better. The revel states that the graph shows what could happen if people take protective measures such as social distancing and self-quarantine during the spread of this pandemic, covid-19. And “does not show how many infected people there are, how many will recover, or how many will die” it is purely to show people why taking proactive measures does matter. I didn't know this when I first looked at the graph. I thought maybe it was a graph from another pandemic such as the Spanish flu. The moderator's comments about the graph made me better understand exactly what it shows. I already knew that with proactive measures we can decrease the number of cases but I didn't know that even with just “moderate interventions, the death rate can be cut in half”. While I was reading the article “Stat Nuggets” I came to understand that the mathematical model “Flattening the Curve Graph” does not predict whether interventions will 100% ensure that people who need medical care won't exceed the health care systems capacity. But the number of cases due to the pandemic won't exceed the number of cases the healthcare system can handle.

raw_comment:
After reading the stat nuggets and "The Reveal", I am wondering why the virus is spreading so rapidly. The article says that the best thing we can do is to close schools, end public gatherings, and make tests more available but we have done that and the virus is still spreading rapidly. Schools across the country are shut down, many for the remainder of the year, and over one-fifth of Americans are under mandatory shelter in place orders. What more can we do to stop the virus?
Mathematically, the virus is still spreading at an exponential rate globally and in the US. When an exponential graph is converted to a logistic model, it typically looks like a straight line. If the line has a positive slope, it is still increasing at an exponential rate. In the US, we are still going up at a positive slope on the logistic model. We haven't even hit the inflection point yet where the virus begins to slow. This mathematical fact makes me question what is going to happen to the country. Are we all going to end up like New York? Are the worst case scenarios of 2/3 of the nation being infected going to play out? All of the data being thrown our way truly scares me and makes me question what we are doing wrong. 
The analogy of the subway in the article was very helpful for my understanding of the model. We as Americans need to listen to our leaders and stay home because if we do not, our "subway" is going to overflow and we will not have enough supplies for everyone.

raw_comment:
After reading the reveal, I realized that an important factor to flatten the curve is changing the mindset of people. The article about which countries have flattened the curve shows how countries like China and South Korea used strict interventions and regulations to slow down or prevent the spread of the virus. Although the graph shows how the curve could stay below healthcare capacity through protective measures, those measures need to be strict and followed by everyone or else the healthcare system will still be overwhelmed like it is now.

Through this theoretical graph based on past data from earlier epidemics, it shows the future of COVID-19 based on our decisions. Although some stores have implemented safety measures for their customers, people who don’t believe in the severity of this pandemic are still holding intimate gatherings of people with slides filled with germs. 

Social distancing itself will not necessarily flatten the curve in the theoretical graph. What is needed is the consciousness of society to be proactive and realize that the parties that they are having may not affect them, but it will be a factor in hindering the progress of healthcare workers and flattening the curve.

To those who want to stay home when they have to work or go to school and aren’t staying home when they are finally told to, please be mindful of all the other people who are working night and day to battle this virus. Stay home, eat some snacks, and binge on some new shows.

raw_comment:
The Reveal and the Stat Nuggets actually confirmed my original response to this graph. Because there is no numerical data in the x or y-axis, the graph is clearly a representation of the world in general, and the effects of social distancing. The Reveal mentions that, "If there were no interventions now, like drive-through testing, cancellation of public gatherings, school closings, and preparation of hospitals, we would exceed our healthcare system’s ability to take care of those who are sick, which would increase the number of deaths. Interventions now will put the brakes on the spread of the infection, will decrease the infection rate, and decrease hospitalizations and deaths."
Only we can control and end the spread of this virus. Social distancing is a real thing, people! Nike has begun a campaign, and their slogan is, "If You Ever Dreamed Of Playing For Millions Around The World, Now Is Your Chance: Play inside, play for the world." This is exactly what we need to do in order to flatten the curve of coronavirus cases. Stay inside, no matter the cost.
The Stat Nuggets are not necessarily stat nuggets in a sense, because the graph is based entirely on what scientists and statisticians have found from previous epidemics. However, I have a feeling that their predictions are indeed correct. With more precautions, we will have fewer cases. It is quite honestly a basic human principle: The more careful you are, the less chance you have of getting hurt.
Stay inside!

raw_comment:
After reading Stat Nuggets, I learned that this graph isn't based on a single epidemic. It's actually a theoretical mathematical model based on previous epidemics. It shows that the more precautions we take, the less the virus will spread. If we don't take precautions, like social distancing, we risk having our health care system surge with patients. This would cause the system to go past its capacity.
After reading The Reveal, I learned that this model was shown to increase awareness about the virus. It was made to show people that they need to change their behavior, and encourage them to take precautions. When we implement protective measures into our community, like closing schools and shutting down large events, we help to mitigate the spread of the virus.

raw_comment:
After reading the reveal I definitely see the positive effects of social distancing more than I did before. The graph is based on theory using data from other epidemics, although we can not accurately predict numbers this is a very accurate representation on how to have less deaths during the virus. 

In my previous comment before the reveal I was skeptical of the virus when  using protective measures lasting longer than if none were used at all. In the text it says that it cannot accurately predict  the duration but they do think the time will last longer using protective measures. I think this has made me see that the important thing is that there will be less overflow in the healthcare system and that is more important than the duration of the virus.

I have learned that social distancing is the best option so that we do not let this virus claim more lives than it has to.

raw_comment:
The article’s perspective and mine seem to be reasonably close. To have less fatality, we must start trying to achieve a blue epi curve. Mitigation is how the red curve will become the blue curve—efforts like social distancing fall under this category. 

The main difference between the two epicures is the likelihood of death, and having the virus more spread out can not overwhelm hospitals. Protective measures have mathematically worked in the past, and they will still work with this virus. Like their examples, it’s a lot harder to spread the virus if we aren’t packed in close quarters. 

With this knowledge, we need to take the social distancing orders more seriously, so we can effectively turn the red into the blue, and finally flatten the curve.

raw_comment:
This reveal shows that the graph is not what we expected. I noticed after reading the article and I looked back at the original graph it seems like we don’t know yet what the number of cases are with and without protected measures. When I originally looked at the graph I did notice that the number of cases without protected measures was lower than the line, which I thought was really strange. In the article it stated “Folks in the preparedness and public health community have been thinking about all of these issues for many years,” Dr. Harris said in an email. “Understanding and managing surge is an important part of preparedness.” 

I think this statement gives me hope that everyone is trying their hardest to keep us safe and prepared through this horrific event. I really agree with Dr. Harris when he said in an email that understanding the surge is a key factor for preparedness, which is totally true because if you fully understand the pandemic, you know what to expect, which helps you be prepared. I am extremely grateful for all scientists and all the people who are keeping us safe through these nerve-racking times

(Part 2)
In North Carolina our governor, Roy Cooper issued school closure until mid May as well as encouraging social distancing and limiting the amount of exposure to large groups of people, challenging the daily lives of Americans. Studies show that using social distancing techniques will decrease the spread of the virus, putting less people at risk. Which may lengthen the amount of time we are exposed to the virus but will keep the number of cases lower never over crowding our hospitals. This is a wise decision because even though some might not take all of the same precautions the sick and recovered will eventually even out.  

So I advise everyone to please not ignore the social distancing recommendations. Keeping a safe distance will help stop the spread and allow others to recover and we can be out on the beach before summer.

raw_comment:
The reveal clarified the purpose of the model to show what will happen if the population takes protective measures.   Instead of displaying numerical values, the model was published to encourage change in our current behaviors to prevent the escalation of calamity.  Implementing protective measures will delay the peak of the coronavirus outbreak.  As a result, the number of cases at a given time will decrease and the length of the epidemic will increase.  Although the duration will increase, a much greater proportion of patients with coronavirus will be able to get adequate care, reducing the number of deaths.  In other words, increasing the duration of the outbreak will ensure that all patients have access to medical care, and the hospitals are adequately equipped with professionals and materials.  

It was also intriguing to learn about how this theoretical mathematical model is developed.  When statisticians and scientists use observations from prior epidemics, I wonder how they choose which epidemics to compare the coronavirus pandemic to.  Furthermore, I wonder if this "Flatten the Curve" model, or a similar one, has been developed for past epidemics.

raw_comment:
We need to slow down the rate of infection with the Coronavirus.  It is probably the most important thing to do right now.  Every day while watching the news with my parents, I hear the Governor of New York, Gov. Andrew Cuomo, begging the U.S. government and private investors to send more medical supplies to New York State, specifically to New York City.  They were not prepared for the COVID-19 outbreak and it hit them the hardest.  As of March 26, there have been 37, 258 confirmed cases of COVID-19 in New York State, and 385 of those people have died.  Doctors and hospitals are so overwhelmed that they are calling for retired doctors and senior medical school students to come and help them.  And because of that, large numbers of people are dying in NY State.  
In my county in North Carolina, there are only 4 confirmed cases of COVID-19, and no deaths so far.  Why?  Because people - for the most part - listened to Governor Cooper.  Practice social distancing, no gatherings of more than 10 people, schools are canceled until May 15, and other precautionary measures have been put into place.  Governor Cooper canceled schools in North Carolina almost a week before Governor Cuomo canceled schools in New York.  And because of that and the other precautions we are taking, we have 4 confirmed cases of the Coronavirus and no deaths.

raw_comment:
I notice that without protective measures, the number of cases increases beyond the healthcare system capacity. However, the time that it takes for the virus to die out is faster than with protective measures. Yet, at the same time, dealing with the virus with protective measures allows for the maximum number of cases to not exceed the healthcare system capacity. 
I wonder why the virus would persist for less time without protective measures. I would think that without protective measures, the number of cases would grow exponentially, since hospitals would be overwhelmed.

“Tracking the Covid-19 Response: How protective measures save lives in the long run”

raw_comment:
I notice the number of cases without protective measures is higher than the number of cases with protective measures. But I also noticed, if we don't use protective measures the virus is expected to take less time than if we use protective measures. Even though avoiding protective measures takes less time, it would be worse than using protective measures because it would include many deaths. There would be more deaths because the healthcare system capacity cannot take care of everyone at once, and healthcare workers would have to decide who they have to fight for. But, if we used protective measures, more people would have a chance of living. I wonder where the United States is on this graph. I feel like the US is somewhere in between, but it mostly depends on where you live. For example, in busy and crowded states like California and New York there are more cases, and they are hit harder than other states like West Virginia or Alaska. A new headline could be: 
"Our Healthcare System Capacity With And Without Protective Measures"

raw_comment:
"Stay Away to Save Lives"

The main thing I notice from this graph is the different charts increase rate. Without protective measures such as social distancing, the number of cases severely increases. That sharp increase overruns the healthcare system which will result in more deaths. Right now, most hospital beds in the U.S. are naturally close to being full. Too many coronavirus infections will mean that there won't be enough ventilators or other equipment to deal with it. You can see an example of this in horrifying videos that are coming out of Italy which show some patients having to sit on floors in bad conditions. 

What I also notice about the graph is that with protective measures we are able to keep the healthcare system stable but the infection rates will last over a long period of time. Although, it will result in less death overall.

I wonder if this decrease in unprotected measures has to due to the fact that we had a late start to protections. 

I wonder how accurate this is. What would this graph look like if it was polled on a different virus?

raw_comment:
Title: Flattening the Curve for a Society Conserved 

I am currently writing from the comfort of my bed at 1:06 pm on a Wednesday - a time typically reserved for test-taking at a forlorn desk or picking up lunch from the school cafeteria. Like me, many have faced alterations in day-to-day routines since the coronavirus outbreak. This is because social distancing measures decrease the rate at which COVID-19, what the CDC deems a global pandemic, proliferates, as reflected in the figure at right. 

The two curves shown depict the relative number of infected individuals with and without protective measures like community isolation. Not only does the overall number of cases decrease tremendously with protective measures, but the peak amount matches the carrying capacity of the health care system. In this way, significantly fewer people will be affected when we self-isolate, as shown in blue, and all of those who do become infected can be treated. In the instance that social distancing and other protective measures do not transpire, however, the avoidable illness will plague thousands more, and there will be a lack of resources to help all those who need aid. I wonder how health care providers will choose which people receive treatment and which do not should this be the case. 

We must unite as a global community to slow the virus’ spread, protecting those more susceptible to the illness and making hospital space for affected individuals. Stay put & stay positive :)

raw_comment:
I noticed two things. As time passes we being to put in more protective measure as we start seeing the true span of the Corona Pandemic. There's a noticeable spike of the number of cases that arose without protective measures, a number which was unsustainable for out current system. Only then did we realize that we needed to take precautions to be able to sustain the system. That's where the second interpretation comes in. Yes we have taken preventive measures, but even so there was a time when we almost surpassed the limit. 
The problem may be dying out now in some areas but that does not make it any more safe. It's barely enough to sustain our healthcare system with preventative measure, so to go against the advice of all health experts and professionals, thinking that everything will be fine is an unjustified belief, because all the facts state otherwise.
I do wonder how many people would have seen the red curve and thought "it's worth it" How many people would have seen that the number of cases dies out faster and risk destabilizing the system for the sake of not taking preventative measures. I wonder if the number of cases goes down because it rose to the point where no one could get sick anymore because everyone was infected, or maybe those who had been infected died out so the number of cases decreased. 
I came up with a name for this graph pretty quickly form the first thing I noticed. "Barely Enough" it's barely enough to keep our healthcare system stable.

raw_comment:
ARE ALL PEOPLE TAKING THE CORONAVIRUS SERIOUSLY?????

I feel like some people are not taking the Coronavirus seriously, and some of them are not taking protective measures such as staying inside, washing your hands frequently, and social distancing. I noticed that the amount of cases without protective measures is through the roof. We as students have all been quarantined in our houses and from school, to prevent the spread of germs. And this graph makes me wonder, is there anything we can do to get people to follow these protected measures? The first thing I think we can do to convince people to follow the protected mesures is to tell them the negative impacts of what could happen  if they did not follow the measures.

In the United States there are 60,653 cases and 819 deaths, which is absolutely and utterly pitiful. I feel like if we all come together and spread awareness about how dangerous the Coronavirus actually is, we can make an actual difference and save hundreds of thousands of lifes. It only takes one person to make a difference, and it doesn't matter how young or old you are, YOU can make a difference in your community or even nation.

raw_comment:
“Our Goal: Merge the Curves”

The graph shown is depicting two different bell curves. The red curve with a narrow standard deviation shows there was an influx in the number of those infected with Coronavirus earlier on. This large surge in people made it very hard for the healthcare system to take care of everyone because there wasn’t as much information on how to contain the virus yet when it first broke out in late December. There was a very high average number of people diagnosed with the Coronavirus in a short period of time when we didn’t take protective measures like washing our hands and social distancing ourselves which resulted in overcrowding at hospitals. Now that people know to social distance themselves, the blue curve with wide standard deviation shows that people are listening to the authorities and implementing protective measures to keep themselves safe and how this helped bring down overcrowding at healthcare facilities. 

What healthcare officials are trying to do is bring down the red curve in a way that doesn’t put the lives of those already infected at risk. We’re trying to gradually bring down the red curve to merge with the blue curve, not run around throwing doctors in every possible direction to strangle the disease out. This spreading out of doctors is exactly what causes overcrowding in hospitals which exceeds healthcare system capacity. The only thing I wonder is where we are on the graph.

raw_comment:
I noticed, in the graph, that without protective measures put in place regarding the health and safety of those who are at risk of becoming sick or haven’t gotten sick yet, the number of cases superseded the amount that the Health care system was able to treat. I also noticed, however, that while the number of cases stayed below the Health care system capacity, it did get pretty close to surpassing the line at the graph’s peak. 

I wonder, after having made my observations, if the number of cases would have diminished completely by now if we had begun to put protective measures in place from the beginning. Would the number of cases have remained controlled and under the line of Health care system capacity? Would people have been as willing to follow precautions put in place so early on in this pandemic as they are now? 

After having studied the graph, a title that I believe to be accurate to the data it represents is “Protective Measures and Our Need to Start Them Early On.”

raw_comment:
How Covid-19 will spread over time with and without protective measures. 

        The red bell curve is the one representing what would occur in a situation in which no preventative measures are taken to reduce the spread. The graph shows a steep incline after the first case, at its peak, it begins to level out showing that the peak infection time is over, exceeding the healthcare capacity by a large margin. On the flip side of this, the pandemic runs its course and dies out much more quickly. Still, the hospitals have been overrun with cases and there will be many casualties to come.
         On the other hand, when certain precautions have been taken the course takes longer but does not result in as many casualties. I wonder though, if we are taking only some preventative measures it would be somewhere around the middle of the two, meaning the hospitals will still be overrun but with not as many casualties due to priorities of who would get help or not, correct? if so why do so many people still not worry about this highly infectious disease?
         About quarantine though, I think that it will help in more ways than one because people are staying home and practicing social distancing, fewer people are at risk. also since fewer people are traveling carbon emissions have most likely been cut by a large portion. I hope that this comment helps people understand the current situation that we are in. I personally found the graph worrying considering our situation at the time.

raw_comment:
This graph shows the importance of taking protective measures against the coronavirus, including social distancing. The first thing I noticed when I looked at it is the drastic difference between the number of cases with and without protective measures. Even doing the simplest things like self quarantining in our homes can make a huge difference on the impact this virus will have on us and the amount of deaths it will cause. 

When I first looked at this graph, I wondered why we would want to prolong this disease when we could just get it over with and everyone could go back to their normal lives. But after thinking about it, I realized it was more important to make sure that we save as many people as possible and don’t overwhelm our medical workers. Flattening the curve may not be the most convenient for most people, but it is better than the alternative where many people die because we did not have the resources to help everyone.  

I wonder how accurate this graph is, and if it’s still possible for us to flatten the curve that much. I don’t know what our healthcare system capacity is or how close we are to reaching it right now, but if we still have time it is important that we do all we can now before it’s too late.

The graph is showing us how the # of cases are affected since the first case of the coronavirus. There are two curves; one is the # of cases since the first case with social distancing (blue) and the other is the # of cases since the first case without social distancing (red). The graph shows that with social distancing, there are less cases, but it’s over a longer period of time. With no social distancing, there are more cases, but the outbeak itself is short lived. It may take longer to get rid of, but social distancing is the best action to take according to this graph.

	A good headline for this graph would be “In It For The Long Haul”. The graph is depicting how social distancing may give the Corona outbreak a longer lifespan, but it restricts the number of cases overall.

raw_comment:
"More Cases Vs. More Quarantine"
When I look at this graph I can immediately see that if the government didn't make us quarantine there would be at least twice as many cases. Along with that, the virus would not span as long of a time because it would go around quicker.  I wonder though, even if people self-quarantine and take good measures in staying safe and healthy, will the virus come back right when we come out of quarantine?

raw_comment:
Favoritism Among Communities
I notice that typically in situations like this, those lacking something are the higher number. In this case, those without protective measures are experiencing more cases of the Corona Virus, than those with protective measures. 
I wonder if this has to do with where people live. Some communities, neighborhoods, or even cities have less access to healthcare, hospitals, etc., than say a city such as New York City does. That makes me sad, because I feel that all people, no matter where they live, should have access to keep themselves healthy.

raw_comment:
The graph is meant to convey the importance of awareness. Of staying safe. Of action.
 The graph is meant to convey, through some abstract metric, not only how many people could become infected with the coronavirus, but how quickly it could rip us apart. To do this, it contrasts the value with a statistic- a projection- of how many people will get infected- of how many will survive and thrive- if we just stay conscious of the situation. If we socially distance ourselves. If we take action.
 Because if we hesitate for a moment, a day, a week. If we stagnate and stall before we quarantine or work from home. If we do nothing to prevent the spread of the coronavirus, it’s spread will look a lot more like the red than the blue, and we’ll see astronomically more deaths.
 This graph is meant to convey a message. Please take action.

raw_comment:
We Fear What We Can’t Control

What I first noticed was the shape of the graphs. Both graphs are basically bell curves, which is something I learned last year in math. The term means the highest point of the graph is the most likely thing that will occur, while the other two sides are equally proportioned. Therefore we are basing our fate off of one point, while the rest is out of our control.

Mainly this graph shows two realities. One predicts what will happen if no cautionary  measures are properly followed, while the other shows what would happen if we were to do the right thing.

Although I wonder what the right thing or answer truly is, because if we were to follow the first than it shows it would be over much sooner. While the “right thing” would carry on much longer, but stay within our health departments control. If we have control then it remains low risk, while if it’s out of control there is no telling other than the outline of the red graph.  So overall it’s a matter of control, much like anything else in the history of our world.

raw_comment:
Why Should We Take Proactive Measures?
I notice that the number of cases is much higher for people who don’t take protective measures where as there are less people infected who take protective measures. It shows how if we just would just participate in things like social distancing and washing our hands for at least forty seconds, we would have less cases and would be able to take care of the people who still got infected. The number of people affected fits right under the healthcare system capacity, which means if we all could just take protective measures, the healthcare system would be able to take care of all those infected instead of only being able to help some. I wonder why people aren’t taking protective measures and why they aren’t staying safe. I just want to know why they think that’s okay. Not only are they at risk but now they have put others at risk as well. I just wish everyone would stay safe and listen to our government so we could get rid of this a lot sooner and get back to normal.

raw_comment:
We are starting to lack the ability to care for patients during the coronavirus. According to the graph, if we take protective measures to prevent the spread of the virus, our healthcare system should just be able to scrape by tending to people as is. But since preventive measures haven’t always been taken, our healthcare system is being overrun by cases, and they have to make the difficult decisions on whom to fight for and whom to give up on because they simply don’t have enough resources. As time wears on, though, I notice how the curve will drop and fall back into our ability to tend to these cases. If we take preventive measures, the spread will be slower, and the care will last longer, but doctors won’t have to choose which lives to save. 
I wonder how the US cases compare to the slopes on this graph, and if there is anything we can do this late in the game to reverse the slope of the cases that hospitals have coming in. It’s terrible to be in the position of a doctor and decide which of the suffocating patients needs most of your attention and to have to run the risk of being in one of their places every day by tending to them. 
My title for this graph would be Controlling Coronavirus: Why Our Healthcare System Needs Our Help.
