raw_comment:
Even though all of this coronavirus-induced chaos may possibly be over sooner if we just go about life as usual (without protective measures), it'd come at a high cost. Our healthcare system is not prepared to handle that many coronavirus cases in so short a period of time. We have neither the equipment, nurses/doctors, nor the beds. However, if we take protective measures such as social distancing, we won't be able to entirely stop the spread of illness, but we'll be able to slow it down enough so that our healthcare system won't be overwhelmed. Clearly, the graph shows that with protective measures, we'll be dealing with this virus for a longer period of time, but I believe that if we spread out the number of cases over more time, there will be fewer deaths and better care.

What I don’t know and wonder about is how this will affect our country and world in other ways, especially economically. I wonder if the economic consequences will be more/less severe if we spread out the number of cases, or if it doesn’t matter. This virus affects our world in so many ways I don’t expect, and I anxiously wonder how we’ll be affected in those (at least for me) unforeseen ways.

With all of these things in mind, I would name this graph The Cost of Not Social Distancing. That sounds kinda blunt and maybe even a little dramatic, but as we can tell from the 2 different curves of the graph, one much steeper than the other, that is what I have gathered from what’s going on in this graph.

However, the amount that healthcare can provide for is still to close for comfort to the number of cases even with the advent of social distance. raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed when looking at this graph was how different the slope of the two curves are. The number of cases rapidly increase on the "without protective measures" graph and are much more spread out on the "with protective measures" graph. I also notice how the without protective measures graph is red, which is a color that symbolizes danger. I think this is an important detail since it could remind viewers of the importance of taking precautions and slowing down the rate of coronavirus cases.

When looking at the "healthcare system capacity" line, I wonder exactly what that means. I know that the importance of slowing down the number of cases is to ensure that hospitals have enough beds and ventilators to treat patients, so this would be one of my guesses.  I also wonder what specific ideas of protective measures were thought of when this graph was being created. Maybe just washing hands often or staying six feet apart from others, or suggestions that are harder to follow like staying home and not hanging out with friends.

Whatever is shown in the reveal, I do know that it's important to do our part by following the CDC's suggestions, because "Flattening the Curve may Pardon our Death Penalty Sentence".

raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice how important it is that we social distance ourselves from others during these trying times. The graph shows that if we socially distance ourselves we can "flatten the curve" and lower the number of cases. However, those that are not taking protective measures to stop the spread of COVID-19 are seeing a huge growth in the total number of cases. Although it takes longer for the number of cases to get to a bare minimum when we social distance, it can be seen that the total number of cases without social distance increases dramatically.
Our government is making tremendous steps to help stop the spread of COVID-19, and I seriously applaud them for the work they are doing. It may take months, but it is better than letting the pandemic wipe out our entire society. I am also proud of the way us Americans are treating this virus. Many of my friends have gone into self-quarantine or are socially distancing themselves. It is remarkable how we have responded. In the end, I hope COVID-19 will be a reminder of how we need to be grateful for everything in life, because it can all be taken from us just like that. If I were to give this graph a headline, it would be, "Flatten the Curve-Be Cool and Don't Be a Fool: Stay Inside".

raw_comment:
Title: "Saved by the Bell (Curve)" 

The graph shows the contrast between number of coronavirus cases without protective measures, and with protective measures, in relation to the level of preparedness of our healthcare system. Without protective measures (self-quarantine, basic hygiene, etc.) the curve is much higher than our healthcare system can handle; this implies hospitals are overpacked, not prepared to take care of that many cases, or lack of medical supplies. However when protective measures are taken and people abide by the "stay at home" rule, the curve flattens and it becomes within the healthcare systems capability. It is also interesting to see the point in time at which the "without protective measures becomes the "with protective measures." (the increase starts to decrease).

raw_comment:
Headline: Is Social Distancing Actually Working?
I noticed that without protective measures we are seeing more cases that the healthcare system cant handle.  I also notice in the graph that with the protective measures we have been told to take we are just under the number of cases the healthcare system can handle. I also noticed that more cases appeared in a short amount of time without protective measures.

Now to answer the headliner, I would say yes, social distancing is helping stop the spread of the virus. Even though we are all hating staying in our houses and not getting to see our friends but I could save people from getting the virus!

.

raw_comment:
This graph shows the importance of social distancing. If we social distance, the amount of people that are infected with the virus at any given time will fall, reducing the demand for medical supplies and vital machinery like ventilators. When people do not socially distance, the infected expose many more people, infecting them and so on. The number of infections increases exponentially, overwhelming the healthcare system. The virus then burns itself out, but not before thousands would be dead from a lack of medical care resources. If social distancing is implemented, the infection rate will slow, making the virus take longer to burn itself out but decreasing the number of cases at any given time. 
The government can only do so much for us. Many complain that the government is not doing enough to help Americans and in some cases that is true. No one should be evicted because they can't go to work because of the virus. But, that being said, many things can be done ourselves to do our part in stopping the virus. The government cannot be blamed for everything. Do your part and stay at home.

raw_comment: The first thing I see in this graph is the big red curve representing “Without Protective Measures” that shoots well past the healthcare capacity line. It peaks as the blue “With Protective Measures” curve is still on the rise, and it dies as the blue one finally peaks but stays under the capacity line. I wonder if it’s worth it to have less control on the Coronavirus (lay back on the protective measures such as social distancing by shutting down businesses and schools and limiting travel) and let it die out faster, or keep in control, under our health care capacity, and let it die slowly. There are pros and cons to both that are pretty well established by the graph. If we let it run its course, then we can get back to our normal lives much sooner, but that means that our healthcare system will not be able to manage the virus and the higher number of infected people as well, so more deaths are likely to occur. On the other hand, our economy will take a heavy blow due to the shut downs lasting a lot longer, but our healthcare system will be able to manage, so less people will die, and we would be a lot safer and in better hands if we were to get it since there are much less cases. Either way, there is much to think about, and not a lot of time to think. The number of cases are on the rise, the death toll is rising, hospitals are running out of room and supplies, and the stock market has taken quite a hit. I would headline this graph as “The Two Faced Coronavirus Debate.”

Part I 
Choosing our Roller Coaster Ride - Which Curve We Achieve is a Life or Death Matter

While most people are impacted by social distancing and hygiene measures to flatten the pandemic curve, it is equally vital to focus on the capacity of our healthcare system. Healthcare system capacity is driven by number of hospital beds and materials needed to treat patients as well as the number of healthcare professionals available. It seems unclear where we are on this curve for the US, my particular state of North Carolina, or even for my local hospital, which only has about 700 beds for a population of 300,000 people.  

If we are early in the curve, do we still have time to act by increasing restrictions on every day life or by adjusting our healthcare system by adding new beds in hotels or dorms? Or, are we on an uncontrollable roller coaster that is climbing to a deadly peak of increasing cases with no chance to change course?  At some point, there will be a point of no return like Italy is experiencing.

raw_comment:
Headline: Why We Need to Practice Social Distancing
     I notice that in the graph, it is predicted that the peak number of cases if protective measures like social distancing are not used is much higher than if protective measures are used. If protective measures are used, it is projected that even the peak number of cases will be below the healthcare system capacity. However, if protective measures are not used, the amount of cases will greatly surpass the healthcare system capacity. This graph seems very similar to what has already happened in some countries.
        In some countries, the prediction relayed by the graph has already taken place. For example, in Italy, protective measures were not used in the widespread manner they should have been used. As a result, hospitals have been overwhelmed. Medical supplies have run short, and heart-wrenching decisions like who will get a life-saving respirator have had to be made. This is the situation that people in the United States are trying to avoid through social distancing. It is predicted that by doing what the United States has done, by using social distancing, peak cases will never exceed the healthcare system's capacity. This has worked thus far, as the capacity of the healthcare system has not been exceeded yet. Even though capacity has not been exceeded, the outbreak is still extremely bad. This leads me to wonder how bad the pandemic would be in the US if protective measures were not put in place.

raw_comment: Looking at this graph, I immediately noticed that the measures being taken to stop the spread of coronavirus (quarantine, shutting down businesses, etc.) should be working. The “Without Protective Measures” curve was higher, and it ended just as the “With Protective Measures” curve peaked. The “With Protective Measures” curve reached only a manageable level for the healthcare system, while the other one exceded the limit which the healthcare system could help. Both curves taper off in the end, though indicating that the virus would end either way. The red curve ended earlier, though. I wonder if this could indicate that just letting the virus run its course would be better for us. Once everyone’s gotten it, there’ll be nowhere else for it to spread, and it’ll just die out. The blue curve ends a lot later, and social distancing would give the virus nowhere to go, but it would take longer to die out because there would still be potential hosts. A potential headline for this graph would be, “How Well America Can Handle Coronavirus”.

raw_comment:
The Importance of Health Care

I notice that when Patient Zero for the Coronavirus was first discovered there were little to no protective measures in place, because of ths the number of Coronavirus cases grew to several thousand cases. I believe that is when the Coronavirus was labeled as a global pandemic and protective measures were put into place.

I wonder if this graph is up to date or if it is showing data for one country or the entire world. I also wonder if we were more prepared would the Coronavirus be as strong as it is now. Too the point that it is destroying the world's economy, closing educational facilities, and raising the unemployment rate to the highest it's been in years. I believe that we will recover from this pandemic and that next time something like this happens again Protective measures will be put into place as soon as possible to avoid another worldwide pandemic.

Flatten the Curve by Staying Inside
One of the first things I noticed was how taking protective measures was prolong the amount of time the pandemic lasts, while without protective measures, the number of cases would decrease quicker. Without protective measures, the healthcare system would overflow with patients and wouldn't be able to handle the maximum, of which the curve reaches.

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, there are two bell curves plotted show what the number of cases of COVID-19 will look like over the timespan from when the first case appeared, to when it is predicted to die-off.  One bell curve shows just how many cases are predicted to appear during a given time without protective measures, while the other bell curve shows what that will look like with protective measures being implemented.  The line represents how many patients and cases the healthcare system is able to treat at any given time.  

It can be seen in the graph, that if no protective measures are taken against preventing the spread of COVID-19 the amount of time which COVID-19 will persist may be shorter, but there will be a much larger amount of cases during its peak, and with such an influx of cases at a given time, there won't be enough medical support to properly treat many of those cases, and leading to many more deaths.  

On the other hand, if protective measures are thoroughly being implemented, the spread of COVID-19 will still occur, but it will happen at a much slower and smaller rate.  Meaning it would persist for longer, but those cases will all be able to get the medical attention they need, and many more people would be able to survive.  By buckling down on taking protective measures can decrease many preventable deaths from COVID-19 due to the shortage of medical attention, and decrease the amount of people infected by COVID-19 at its peak.

raw_comment:
Stay Home, Save a Life

I wonder how many people look at this and say "Why are we practicing social distancing? It's only hurting us." I can understand how that misconception is common, as it appears that taking protective measures elongates the lifetime of the virus, but if you look closer, the longer the virus is around, the more victims our healthcare system can treat.

Upon examination of this graph, it is evident that without protective measures, our healthcare system will be grossly overwhelmed. For teenagers, this virus isn't very lethal. However, just because it isn't lethal, doesn't mean that you won't need medical attention if you do contract it. The other day, one of my friends talked about catching Coronavirus just to "get it over with." As nice as this may sound for teens, it can be deadly for society. Even if COVID-19 doesn't kill you, just a little bit of fluid in your lungs can warrant hospitalization. If you, an unsympathetic teen, is taking up resources in a hospital, you are denying those services to someone who is at risk of dying from this virus.

So, stay home. Don't go out with your friends, to the grocery store, or expose yourself to anyone else unless you have to. I know, social distancing sucks, but you're doing it to protect the people and healthcare officials in your town. If this graph tells us anything, it isn't that social distancing is hurting us, but that it MUST happen if we want to overcome this virus with as little casualties as possible.

raw_comment:
Stop Touching Me! Stop Touching Yourself! Stay At Home!
Yes, we know that the coronavirus is going around and that it is serious. We understand that people are scared for themselves and their loved ones, but that does not mean we leave our houses and show that we are panicking. All we are doing is putting ourselves and others at more risk to catch the virus and give it to the ones we love when we go back home. As you can see in the graph, without protective measures, the number of cases are going to exceed what the healthcare system can handle, which means that more people are going to die. With protective measures, even though it will last a little bit longer than without protective measures, it stays below what the healthcare system can handle, which means less casualties. I say we are somewhere in the middle of both estimated sets of data because although we are making sure we have the right equipment to fight off diseases, we are still going outside of our houses to do so, which means we are still touching things that others have touch and who knows if that person sneezed or coughed all over their hands before touching objects that others have to touch. I work at Harris Teeter so all I see is people, some with no protection on them, walking around touching things and putting them back, others have face masks and gloves on, smart. Simple solution and request, stop touching things, wash your hands, and stay inside if you have no valid reason to leave the house.

raw_comment: In this graph, it is showing the difference in the number of cases depending on how we deal with it. This graph depicts the scary reality of the coronavirus; with or without protective measures, there is a high chance of being infected. The non-protective measure curve, however, has a percentage of people who do not fit in the healthcare system capacity. Once again, this statistic shows how bad the pandemic has gotten in terms of containment.
 Somewhere out there, a person with coronavirus symptoms may not receive the help they need, a harsh consequence for not taking adequate protective measures. For many people, not taking protective measures may be a matter of ignorance, however, some people may not have had a choice. A sizable percentage of the companies in America do not provide sick-leave pay, and in the midst of the pandemic, some people may not be able to lose income. As a result, these companies have created an unsafe workplace environment and have contributed to the overload of our healthcare system. 
Our society needs to come together and ensure that no working-class citizen feels as if they are being backed into a corner and forced to work.

raw_comment: I noticed that while this graph is a model that was made prior to the epidemic, the pattern displayed with both the hypothetical scenarios seems to be pretty accurate based on what has played out with the virus and its transmission. I also noticed that the blue section labeled “with protective measures” manages to conveniently peak just below our labeled “healthcare system capacity”. I have no doubt that this model is accurate in showing how protective measures impact the quantity of cases, but I wonder how the highest point just so happens to be right below health care capacity. Of course, this is what we want to see, but I wonder if even with all of our protective measures in place we still might go over that dotted line. I don’t believe it would be as drastic as without our protective measures, but I still think it is more likely than some of us believe. I don’t want to be pessimistic, but I think people should be prepared for a potentially compromised health care system even if our efforts to distance are strong. I think a disease like COVID-19 is contagious enough to overcome our preventative measures even if they go surprisingly well. raw_comment:
My first thought when I heard news reporters say we need to practice social distancing was, "how ridiculous is this?" I was upset that school was cancelled, and I was upset how much this virus has changed millions of lives as well as my own. This graph chages my perspective by showing in actuality, how important social distancing really is.

   This graph represents how the number of COVID-19 cases suddenly spiraled and went back down without any protective measures, and it also shows the gradual growth and decline of cases. This leads me to wonder, in the long run, does it truly make a difference to take such big precautions? The graph shows the huge impact the virus had withought precautions, but it also shows how fast it stopped affecting people. Why not just let everyone contract the virus and live through it? 

   I realize that's a rather insensitive question, but it's one that I have heard many friends and family wonder about. Although I question the ways we are going about this pandemic, I do believe that right now, social distancing and self isolation is the best possible way to get through it. Society has never dealt with a virus like this in the 21st century. It is a new thing that we are all trying to navigate. I find it interesting how society has been able to come together and fight against this virus.

raw_comment:
"Stay Home, For Everyone"

I noticed the differences that protective measures make. Without protective measures, our healthcare system would become quickly overwhelmed and would be unable to deal with the influx. of patients. With protective measures like social distancing and constant hand washing, the number of patients just barely stays under the capacity.

I wonder what amount of protective measures are enough to flatten the curve. Although many people are doing what they can to keep themselves and others safe, there are still people who don't believe in the seriousness of the situation and are still having large gatherings. I wonder how much the curve is affected by that and what else we can do to flatten the curve and decrease the burden on the healthcare workers on the frontline.

raw_comment:
I notice how much flatter the curve gets when protective measures are used against this virus. It is also interesting to see the health care capacity line. I have heard on the news many times about countries like China and Italy having to turn away patients because of the number of people that have the virus. This is really concerning, but I think it is important to hear, the same thing could happen in our country if we are not careful. Now is the time to use protective measures to flatten the curve and make sure our healthcare system is able to provide for everyone that needs to be provided for.

I also find it interesting and surprising that with protective measures the virus will actually last longer than if no protective measures are taken. I find this really odd, I would think that protective measures would both lower the number of cases and the amount of time it is around for. I am very interested to see why this is when the reveal for the graph comes out.

 I wonder if people will participate in social distancing after seeing this. Although social distancing is not fun it really is necessary in lowering the amount of people getting the virus. I also wonder what other protective measures we can use to flatten the curve, the only one that I have consistently heard is social distancing but if there are other ways to slow the spread I would be interested in hearing them. 

I think a good headliner would be, ‘We can flatten the curve.’

raw_comment:
Headline: Corona Cases
I notice in this graph that there is a severe difference in the people without protective measures and the people with protective measures. I notice that if we don't take precautions against this virus, the number of cases could increase. We all need to practice social distancing during this time, but also keeping good hygiene by washing our hands, taking showers, and cleaning up your house. The CDC, The President, and all news networks are telling us to stay inside and keep distance from other people. Looking back at the graph it looks like people who are handling this virus with precaution have a much lower risk of getting it. Some things that I wonder about this graph is how accurate it is. There are no numbers on this graph to give an accurate representation of the people taking and not taking protective measures. I also wonder when the last time the graph was updated, as the cases are starting to increase more.

raw_comment:
By looking at the graph, I notice there are two curves being studied, if you may. One curve looks at the growth of the virus without taking protective measures, and the other with taking protective measures. It seems from the data that the cases will fall back to zero faster without taking protective measures, but the healthcare system capacity will be exceeded. By using protective measures, it will take longer for the cases to fall to zero, but we will not exceed the healthcare capacity.

It’s important to understand that this data is all theoretical. Whoever compiled it can’t measure how the number of cases will change when the healthcare capacity is exceeded. The data seems to suggest there won’t be any changes to the curve after the capacity is exceeded. I wonder with the almost exponential growth of the virus, in addition to the healthcare capacity being exceeded, what that would be like on any scale. The data suggests that eventually the cases will go back down, but I truly wonder, would they? If we have no ability to contain the virus, who is to say the number of cases won’t stop going up? I fear that our healthcare system does not have the ability to handle such a vast number of cases, and if it does collapse, we would be in a crisis that the world has never seen before. The scientific community unanimously agrees that the priority has to be containment. Not doing so could be deadly. A fitting title could be: “Healthcare System Capacity Exceeded. Is it Worth it?”

raw_comment:
The number one goal right now should be to flatten the curve- to lower the amount of cases of people with the Coronavirus. And as this graph and research proves, the number one method for doing so is to practice social distancing. At first glance at the graph shown, I see that if we don't, as a whole society, stay home and socially distance ourselves from others, the number of cases will only continue to rise and hospitals will run out of the needed room and tools to treat people. Every human being must be more aware than ever now that their decisions really do affect others in a life or death manner. 

I applaud the countless healthcare workers out there risking their lives in hospitals, and as the graph shows, we can do our part to help them by staying home so that they don't have to worry about running out of treatment options and beds for sick people. There are many other ways to stay in contact and remain connected with people who you care about virtually. That being said, I don't think distancing ourselves from other people should be referred to as social distancing in every case. Rather, it could just be called distancing. 

Without protective measures, the graph proves that the amount of people diagnosed with COVID-19 will keep rising significantly. In order to stop that, each individual must do their part to stay healthy and safe. This means washing your hands, sanitizing objects that you use frequently, and keeping your distance from people to flatten the curve.

A catchy headline for this graph could be “Does washing your hands really help” or “ how you can help flatten the curve”

raw_comment:
The news, the CDC, the president, everyone is telling us to stay inside and socially distance ourselves. With the introduction of protective measures, the amount of cases is a small slope that stretches on as time goes on. 

While without protective measures, it's a shorter amount of time but an overflow for the health community. The virus does spread, and by the graph, it's evident, but the difference between the two is that one jeopardizes the health care system, while the other one doesn't. 

The virus will be around, but how you spread it out could help everyone in health care. With social distancing, small groups (like a family) are still at risk for infection, but this is better than tons of college students at the beach having the risk instead. The mass gathering is how this virus will spread, and this is why the curve is so high.  If you follow protective measures though you will have a much better time getting the proper health care you need.

raw_comment:
Serve America and Flatten the Curve
     The first thing I noticed was how taking preventive measures will make the pandemic last a longer period of time, therefore my immediate thought was “Why would we want to make it longer?” But when I studied the graph a little more, I noticed the dashed line, showing the capacity that hospitals can care for. People who get critically sick will need immediate care in the hospital and since COVID-19 is a respiratory illness, they will need ventilators, which are in limited supply in all hospitals. 
    Are we taking enough preventative measures to efficiently flatten the curve and have room for all who need care in hospitals? Where I live in Wilmington, North Carolina, I would like to say yes, we are taking a lot of preventative measures. Schools and most workplaces were shut down before we had any confirmed cases and all get-togethers of over 10 people were banned by the governor, Roy Cooper. On the other hand, places like New York City and Seattle are already flooded with cases, so I wonder if their hospitals are overflowing with cases yet. In situations where hospitals overflow, I painfully wonder how officials choose who does and doesn’t get the ventilator needed to save their life. I wouldn’t wish for my worst enemy to be a part of that situation, no matter their role.

raw_comment:
I notice that without protective measures, the number of cases of a disease will rise much quicker, reach a much higher maximum, but then decrease quicker. Weirdly enough, using protective measures actually prolongs the lifespan of the disease, but ensures that the peak of the disease is not nearly as high. 

I wonder what the area under each of the curves, or the integral, is, because that would tell us how many total cases there were in each scenario regardless of time. This would tell us whether protective measures are actually decreasing cases, or if protective measures simply flatten out the curve. 

Despite the graph possibly leading people to believe protective measures are actually hurting us, I think protective measures are integral to stopping the severity of a virus. With protective measures, our healthcare systems can still manage all of the cases, even though it is over a longer period of time. Without protective measures, many of those cases during the maximum are without healthcare because the healthcare system is already overloaded. This would lead to more possible deaths because of no medical treatment. A good title to this graph would be "Stay Inside. Your Life and Others' Depend On It."

raw_comment:
In the graph, I notice that with protective measures, the number of cases goes down significantly. I also noticed that there is a line for our healthcare capacity. This limit requires protective measures to be taken during a disease so all patients can be cared for. However, without protective measures, there is a large spike that goes well beyond healthcare capacity. What is curious about this graph is that without protective measures, the disease decreases rapidly compared to with protective measures. Where the disease ends for the red portion is where there is a small spike with protective measures. This reminds me that the potential for everyone to get the disease is much more prolonged under quarantine. Based on the graph, it seems like the same amount of people could get infected either way. Yet what can be controlled here is how many can get treatment. I wonder what the graph would look like if it showed casualties in both situations. There would likely be far less with protective measures than without, showing that despite the people infected remaining inevitably the same, it is important that measures are taken so that hospitals are not overflowed. Does this mean our country is not prepared in terms of healthcare? If, in a perfect scenario, we had very expansive tools and space within hospitals, could protective measures not need to be taken? 

Societal Measures Must Be Taken to Sustain Hospital Capacity in the Event of a Disease

raw_comment:
How Important is Protection?
According to the graph, I notice using protective measures can make you less likely to get the virus, but definitely does not prevent you from getting it. While there is a difference in the number of cases regarding the use of protective measures and without, I wouldn’t say it is drastic. It’s up to us whether or not you use protective measures, but in reality, how much does it really help?

I wonder if it’s even worth it to take the time to take these protective measures. For all I know, I could have it right now. Of course, most of the time the answer would immediately be yes, take the time to use protection because you never know. I believe that some people would debate this though. At the end of the day, everybody has their own decision and it’s up to them.

raw_comment:
Flattening the Curve
I notice in this graph that the world's healthcare system's resources won't be enough if we don't take protective measures. I've seen this graph before. My parents sent it to me when the Coronavirus first started getting serious around our area. It stresses that washing hands and reducing contact with others besides whoever you live with will flatten the curve of cases, making it possible for the system to cover all of them. 
I wonder just how quickly this would happen if everyone really started staying inside and following other safety measures such as not touching your face and washing hands before every meal. It honestly might happen very fast if everyone starts to listen and stay in their homes.

raw_comment:
The Importance of Protection

I notice that the featured graph deals with the Coronavirus.  It shows how important it is to obey the government's protective measures and procedures they are communicating to the people of the United States.  I infer this by understanding the graph's labels.  If we do not follow protective measures, the number of patients with Covid-19 will exceed the capacity of our nation's Healthcare system.  However, by obeying the protective measures communicated to us, our Healthcare system will be able to sustain itself and not become overwhelmed by patients who test positive for Covid-19.  According to this graph, avoiding protective measures will mean that the number Covid-19 cases will decrease quickly and the virus will not be around as long if we do follow protective measures.  I infer this will be because there will be many more deaths due to the limited amount of patients our Healthcare system can support.  These deaths will be attributed to the lack of ventilators and hospital staff available to treat them.

I wonder how long it is until the Coronavirus is eradicated from the United States and ultimately the world.  It is said that a cure for the virus could take over a year to develop.  I wish there were labels on the graph that estimated how long it could potentially be until the virus is gone.

Although with protective measures, it's close to the capacity at least with these measures, we can make sure everyone gets treated.

         I wonder what other protective measures besides social distancing and washing are hands we can take. I feel they should put us on quartine in are homes as soon as possible. Yes, it's not ideal, and most people would go crazy. But we could stop the spread of this virus and be able to go back to our lives.

raw_comment:
Social distancing or social dooming?
The first thing I noticed on this graph is the drastic difference between the amount of people who got the virus that used protective measures and the ones that didn’t. Protective measures are very important to slow the spread to others as well as protecting yourself from getting the virus. When the virus first started I noticed that there were large numbers of people with the virus that didn't take protective measures and a small amount that did. This is most likely due to people  not taking the virus seriously or not knowing that they had the virus. As the virus progresses more people are taking precautions and the amount in red goes lower, but protective measures in blue still increases because the virus has increased so dramatically that even some of the ones that took precaution still ended up with the virus, but it never crossed the dangerous healthcare system capacity. 

If everyone would have taken protective measures at the start of the virus, would it have died out at the start? Or would people still get it even though they took protective measures like in the graph in blue?

"What benefits social distancing has to offer"

raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice that the number of cases when safety precautions are taken is significantly lower than when they’re not. The curve is a lot smaller and under the health care capacity. When citizens practice these precautions such as social distancing, then there will be more healthy patients. Those without these safety measures are infected a lot quicker, causing the amount of people infected to rise over health care capacity. This will result in lack of resources to help these patients and a decline in economic progress.

When I look at the graph, I wonder how many people does it take who aren’t following protective measures for this graph to change or be inaccurate? What can we as citizens do besides staying home to flatten this curve or shorten this pandemic even more?

A catchy headline for this graph could include: “Corona is controlled by you.” or “What can washing your hands really do?”

raw_comment:
Is Protection Really Needed?
I notice in this graph that if we don’t take protective measures to control this virus then Our Healthcare Systems will not be able to support it anymore. If we do not protect ourselves by washing hands, self isolating ourselves, and keeping social distances when we must go out then cases will continue to grow and things will be out of control due to the Healthcare System capacity limit being excited. But if we inflict those protective measures upon ourselves and encourage others to do so as well we will be able to control and contain this virus to some extent. And we will hopefully be able to prevent more deaths and more illnesses, saving many lives. 

Looking at the graph I wonder how accurate this data is. Is this fresh or is this old data. I'm curious to know if they use one country as a source of data for this graph or is this information coming from a world collection. Of course we have been told by our country's government and our local government about what protective measures they suggest for us to take, but what protective measures is this graph talking about? Are there suggestions out there that we haven't been informed of that could help us slow this virus down.

raw_comment:
When I first see this graph, I realize that protective measures don't really stop people from getting the virus, it just slows the spread. Without protective measures, there is a large spike in people who get the virus, but then the amount of people who get it slowly come to a halt. 

I think protective measures would still be a good thing to practice, because we wouldn't want hospitals overrun with patients, and it would give us time to figure out more solutions to this issue.

I wonder if we worked fast enough in implementing protective measures, it would flatten the curve even more.

raw_comment:
I’ve noticed that the beginning of this graph is showing us that the lack of protective measures is what took the spreading and number of cases so high so quickly. This overflowing of the capacity of healthcare did decrease afterwards, but a bit slower. Those who were able to access protection have still had the virus spread to them, but the number of cases is very different according to the model. The number of cases is drastically lower, and under the capacity of healthcare needs. What did interest me is that those with protective measures had the virus for a longer time, which shows me that the model might be saying that the spreading of the virus took longer between people who were taking measures to avoid the sickness. I wonder how likely the spread of the virus is between those with protective measures and what the actual data between the length of these two types of cases looks like, so we could better understand if there were ways to better prevent our communities from getting sick and the behavior of the virus itself.

How do we prevent a disease that could be anywhere we go?

raw_comment:
1.) Based in the Protective Measures Graph, I noticed that with said protective measures, the number of cases remains below the healthcare system's capacity with a smaller curve. These protective measures most likely consist of practicing social distancing and washing your hands frequently. It is shown in the graph that practicing these methods will result in higher amounts of recovered, healthy patients. Without these measures, the curve is significantly larger, exceeding the healthcare system's capacity. What is “flattening the curve?”  What curve?  Why do we want to flatten it?  What do you notice and wonder about the effect of protective measures on the spread of the coronavirus?  Please recognize that this graph shows a model and not data.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph. 

We encourage students to respond to other students.  We expect teachers to respond to their students as well other students from around the world.

Before Friday, we will reveal the article that included this graph and much more.

A headline I have come up with based on this graph is “Respect the Capacity, Use Protection!”

raw_comment: I notice that the red curve exceeds the rate of cases that the Healthcare system can take in. The blue curve just barely stays under the healthcare line and slowly starts to recede. One thing I wonder about is why the cases decrease faster for the non-protective measures compared to the With protective measures. Could this downward path possibly be caused by cases that result in death from overexposure? Could it be that people heal faster when unprotected? If so what's the science behind it? From this graph, we can confirm what scientists have been telling us about social distancing and it's correlation to having less of a chance of catching the virus as opposed to continuing life as normal. The red curve looks like at it's peak it has risen twice the size of the blue one. I also wonder about how this graph would change if it were to display the numbers in different countries or states? Is one country/state doing better at protecting themselves than the other? If so what are they doing? Does the environment of the place affect results? A headline for this article could be, "How the coronavirus outbreak is effecting the Healthcare system and what you can do to stop it?" An additional shorter one may be, "How taking protective measures can save the Healthcare System!"

raw_comment: I noticed that this graph looks like it's talking about the coronavirus. This is because it looks like it's talking about cases of a disease and it is from the CDC, which I believe is an institute about containing diseases. The graph also looks like an example of "flattening the curve" which not only controls the disease but also doesn't wear out the energy of healthcare workers. However, if we do not flatten the curve, there would be chaos and exhausted healthcare workers, similar to now. I wonder if there would be a situation where human existence would end because of a pandemic since some people can't control it immediately. I think this could be possible since nowadays, in my opinion, society reacts more slowly to serious problems. This graph is comparing to how it would be if we took protective measures and if we didn't and putting an additional line to let us see how much we're exhausting the healthcare system because of our response to the sudden disease. The catchy headline I would suggest for this graph would be "Why Not Be Safe? It'll Benefit Everyone".

raw_comment:
One thing I noticed is that when protective measures are taken, there are fewer cases of coronavirus--about half of the cases as there would be if there were no protective measures. With protective measures, the cases are more spread out, allowing the healthcare system to be able to handle everyone who has the virus. Without protective measures, many people get the virus at once, and the healthcare system is unable to handle so many cases.

I'm wondering why the healthcare system capacity line hasn't changed over time, as more people are affected by the virus I feel that the healthcare capacity line would go down. I can also understand how the line would go up, if more hospitals are built or more medical staff are hired, but I'm wondering why it stayed the same over time.

A headline that could describe this graph is, "Why Protective Measures Are So Important" or "Our Healthcare System Can Only Handle So Much," because the graph displays how, even if taking protective measures, the healthcare system can only hold so many people.

raw_comment:
One thing I noticed is that when protective measures are taken, there are fewer cases of coronavirus--about half of the cases as there would be if there were no protective measures. With protective measures, the cases are more spread out, allowing the healthcare system to be able to handle everyone who has the virus. Without protective measures, many people get the virus at once, and the healthcare system is unable to handle so many cases.

I'm wondering why the healthcare system capacity line hasn't changed over time, as more people are affected by the virus I feel that the healthcare capacity line would go down. I can also understand how the line would go up, if more hospitals are built/more medical staff are hired, but I'm wondering why it stayed the same over time.

A headline that could describe this graph is, "Why Protective Measures Are So Important" or "Our Healthcare System Can Only Handle So Much," because the graph shows how, even if protective measures are taken, the healthcare system can barely hold everyone.

raw_comment:
I noticed immediately the relationship between the x and y axes (x=time since first case; y=number of cases). Protective measures impact the number of cases. The healthcare system capacity remains the same. The number of cases does not surpass the healthcare system capacity with protective measures; the number of cases is much higher when there are little or no protective measures and this also surpasses the healthcare system capacity. This means that without protective measures there are more or too many cases that are unable to be treated. With more protective measures, the healthcare system capacity is not surpassed because there are less cases. 

I wonder if countries with protective measures could have a resurgence in cases later. I am writing from South Korea and we have already peaked and our healthcare system survived. But now since students are returning from infected countries abroad we worry if they will cause the numbers to go up again even though we have protective measures in place. 

My headline: Absence of Protective Measures Stresses Healthcare Systems

raw_comment:
One observation that came to mind when I looked at the graph was that the blue section (the section that represents taking protective measures) lasts longer then the red section, but the rate consistently remains under what the healthcare system can handle. Whereas the red section (the section that represents without protective measures) goes above the healthcare limit almost forthwith. I have concluded that this graph is showing the readers how social distancing does not evidently decrease the spread of viruses, but slows the spread to a rate were our healthcare can provide for the sick people. The blue section demonstrates the spread of viruses slowed, so that it can be handled, and the red section represents everyone getting ill at once, causing the sick people to go into a state of non-provision. 
One wondering that I have about this graph is if social distancing will, along with slowing the spread of viruses, reduce the amount of people infected with the viruses. I am wondering this because there seems to be around the same amount of area covered by both of the sections. I am curious as to social distancing will just slow the spread, or if it will reduce the contamination. 
The above graph is representing how social distancing can slow the spread of viruses so that the healthcare system is not overwhelmed by the amount of cases, and can provide care and treatment for the infected people, reducing the fatalities.

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph is showing how public health measures, like social distancing, will decrease the number of people that will contract this disease at once; however, it is also suggesting that without these measures, we could get over this epidemic much faster. 

What this graph is also saying is that our health care systems will be able to manage the number of patients better if we slow the spread of this disease; therefore, we need to use precautions. This seems to be the goal of our healthcare systems and our country collectively so that they are able to save and help as many people as possible. 

However, when I look at the red curve, I really question if that is the best thing for our country. If we implement all of these precautions, it looks as if its going to take two to three times longer to get over this disease; but, if we don't use protective measures, we will be able to return to a normal lifestyle much faster. This is an appealing option because right now, the economy is really struggling and it's only getting worse everyday. This is a hard thing to decide on, but I like that our country is choosing to help as many people as possible.

In the end, the two models equal the same number of cases, but in different ways. I wonder what the exact number of cases is that overwhelms the healthcare system? Why does the Virus appear to linger for a longer amount of time when there are protective measures, shouldn't those precautions be limiting the number of cases overall? Headline-
“How are protective measures helping people stop COVID-19?”


I noticed that the x-axis of the graph is the time since the first case and the y-axis is the number of cases. There are two areas of data in this graph. I also notice that the HealthCare Capacity can only help half of the people who didn’t take PM. When I look at this graph I wonder why the people who didn’t take PM cases spiked at first but are now non-existent.

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I notice that without protective measures, we would have many more cases at a much earlier time, while by taking protective measures, we would have less cases over a more steady and manageable period. Also, by not taking protective measures, we would end up going beyond the healthcare system capacity, and thus we would lessen our ability to take care of the ill. But if we took protective measures, we could greatly mitigate the number of cases and work within a functioning healthcare system. I wonder, can we truly work within the healthcare capacity? Honestly, some people aren't taking this virus seriously, so their just giving the virus a chance to spread. And we're running out of necessary supplies, such as hand sanitizer and masks. In order to fight against COVID-19, we need to learn social distancing and conserve important supplies.

Catchy Headline
"Be Smart and Be Safe. The Reality of COVID-19"

Ight homies, stay safe. We can get through this:)

raw_comment:
I notice that between the two graphs, the number of cases stay the same while the rate of change is different. The graph without protective measures reaches its peak of cases roughly half as fast than the with protective measures graph. I notice that the Healthcare system capacity lies about halfway through the without protective measures graph and just above the top of the with protective measures graph. This tells us that if we do not follow protective measures like social distancing, we could face a serious problem. We even cut it close when following these acts of distancing. If we do social distance, it slows down the spread rate, giving the healthcare system more time to help the infected. If we do not, there will be almost double the amount of cases that the healthcare system can care for, resulting in many issues. 
I wonder how much longer the timeline of citizens who stay home, wash their hands, and avoid travel is than the timeline of the citizens who ignore these guidelines. I wonder if numbers added to the graph would have made it easier to understand. Did the creators of this graph not know what numbers/dates to put on the x and y axis? 
My catchy headline: "Flattening the curve one 'cancelled plan' at a time"

raw_comment:
I notice that by applying protective measures, including social distancing, the number of cases is just barely under Healthcare system capacity. I also noticed that the distribution of number of cases without protective measures is roughly normal, while the number of cases with protective measures is uni modal, thin-tailed, and slightly asymmetric.

I wonder what the scale is for the number of cases and the scale for time since first case. I also wonder what the CDC deems to be the first case of Corona virus and when it happened. Most of all, I wonder if people do not adhere to struct protective measures, will the healthcare system capacity quickly overflow, or did they account for people not following the measures.

I think what is going on in this graph is the CDC showing a best case scenario graph where most if not all people follow the safety procedures. I bet they are showing this in order to help reassure people that we can overcome the disease but also that if people do not adhere to the protective measures, it could quickly become and issue.

My Catchy Headline: "Pushed To The Very Brink"

raw_comment:
I notice in the graph that due to the rapid transmission of this disease after Dec 2019 and currently no vaccine or medicine to cure this disease, the goverment is falling short of resources. After the sudden rise in the case, especially in Wuhan and Italy where the hospital are lacking enough care units, many government have asked their citizens to get into quarantine even if one is not infected in order to reduce the speed of transmission of this virus. As people are now more aware and taking precautions to keep themselves at home, wearing masks and washing hands, the number of cases per day has reduced and falling within the resources available for the healthcare system.
I wonder for how long the COVID-19 transmission chain will go on and when that stage would come when the graph will approach zero.
Headline: "Moving from uphill to plateau of Covid-19"

raw_comment:
I notice that without protective measures being taken there are a large number of cases that exceed the healthcare system capacity dramatically. Although the outbreak would be far more severe and hazardous without protective measures being taken, it would go away much sooner. This graph appears roughly normal, as there are few cases when the first case appears, the number of cases dramatically increases at a rapid rate, then decreases at a rapid rate to settle down at 0 again. I also notice that with protective measures being taken there is a reduced amount of cases that never exceeds the healthcare system capacity. The virus tends to linger much longer with protective measures being taken. Although, the number of cases is spread evenly across a long period of time since the first case appeared, the graph appearing somewhat neutral.  
I wonder why the red graph of the no protective measures stops so much earlier than the blue graph of the protective measures? Does the red graph only last a small duration of time because everyone dies at this point? I also wonder how long the virus would last if everyone in the US now started taking protective measures? A good headline for this graph would be, "COVID-19 Cases Continue to exceed healthcare system capacities."

raw_comment:
At first glance, I noticed that the number of cases with protective measures is already almost at hospital capacity. Also, the peak of cases with protective measures is right in the middle of the graph, the peak of the number of cases without protective measures is right at the beginning, so that means it will get very bad very fast. After looking at this graph, I believe that protective measures are very important and they need to be taken in order for the healthcare system to treat the coronavirus in a timely manner. 
I am wondering, after seeing how much trouble Italy is in, is the graph without protective measures based on Italy’s situation? It seems like Italy got very bad very fast, due to the percentage of older people in their population and the fact that parts of Italy are still developing and probably many other factors. 
In the graph, the main headline that is going around is to “flatten the curve”, that is because the main idea of this graph is to continue taking protective measures such as self-quarantine in order to keep the number of cases of coronavirus under the hospital's maximum capacity. If that doesn’t happen, many more people will get sick all around the same amount of time, which would flood the hospitals leading to a lack of resources and possibly many more deaths or major cases. My catchy headline would be “don’t make a mountain out of a molehill”

raw_comment:
I notice that both curves have the same area, but different distributions. It is because of the protective measures that the distribution is different; this difference is critical to health care system capacity. With a wider distribution, the probability of the health care system to care for all the cases goes up significantly. 
I wonder what a curve that represents less preventative and protective measures would look like. I also wonder what a curve without major measures (like social distancing) might look like in comparison to these two curves. Additionally, I wonder what one of these curves would show about the distribution of cases over time. 
Headline: Distributing COVID-19: Protective Measures Lengthen the Distribution Cases Over Time

One thing I notice is that the red curve is above the healthcare system capacity line but the blue line is below the capacity line.

I wonder if people realize that social distancing will not decrease the number of cases as a whole but that it will spread out or lengthen the time it takes to spread meaning hospitals will be able to treat everyone more effectively/effeciently. 

For a headline, I would suggest "Social Distancing: Spacing Out the Spread of COVID-19"
